Here's the plot of my first and utterly terrible RPG Maker game that I tried to make. I never released it (still have it though, I play through it every so often for laughs). Lots of unbalanced stuff, broken and unfinished events, horrible maps, etc.
Spoiler:
Plot of my first RPG Maker game
The first one I did was called "Magical Castle~Battle Knight". The title hardly has any relation to the actual game, it was supposed to be "JRPG-like" from the viewpoint of someone who never played a JRPG. Anyway, you start off as Ralph in an unnamed town. You talk with your friend Joseph, and do a bunch of complaining about how you want adventure. He brings up a rumor about some magic crystals that are "powerful and kingdom ruling", and are supposedly on another continent where a famous battle known as the "Tri-Battle" was fought. You need to get permission to leave the village, so as you are wandering around you find an elf about to be sacrificed in one of the village houses. You free her from the clutches of her captor, and find some magic crystal pieces in a crack in the wall. You then go to clan leader, Master Chung, and ask him to let you leave and search for the "Six Crystals of Power"
*
. After training with some of the village guard, he mentions you will be fighting the forces of Dragoth, who is some evil guy that wants to destroy the kingdom.
*
He sends you to some place called the Wood Kingdom, with the main castle. On your way there, you can stop by a village full of random crap
*
. Inside, you talk with the king and the elf conveniently speaks up, mentioning the fact that she is an elf and that's important. The king tells you to go to the Snow Kingdom in the south
*
and the plot ends there as it was never finished. There is other stuff shoved in this tiny castle, like a guy who lets you hire more party members, a skeleton called Diablo, and a blond haired guy called "The WoW-God".
*
Both of them give you very difficult quests, sell overpowered and absurdly expensive gear, overuse the word "epic", and make all sorts of bad pop-culture references. The game basically separates from the established "lore" at this point, as this screenshot proves below.
On top of all this absurdity, there is a tower on the world map that if you go in, you can't leave. Diablo traps you in Hell, which looks a lot like an Inn but filled with skeletons and lava. Ralph's ordeal and the tower are directly referenced in another one of the games I am working on, which took the good ideas from Magical Castle~Battle Knight and made them into something much better and cohesive. No matter how bad a project is, you can still find pieces that can get used.
* You didn't know the name of the crystals before, but now you do for sake of exposition.
* The kingdom of what, you don't know.
* There's a kid who's scared of a spider, a dragon statue comes to life and fights you twice in a row, and monster who is discriminated against and just wants to live in his house in peace.
* You heard that right. Geography is no concern to magic kingdoms.

I do think graphics matter quite a bit. I’m pretty firm in that position and always have been.
100% default characters and tile sheets would be unremarkable at best,
but
100% custom assets can still look pretty lousy if you’re not using them well.
There is effort that needs to be employed regardless of what is being used. The RTP style of graphics absolutely can be made to look better and completely customized artwork does not automatically make the game visually appealing.
Effort is a pretty big nuance here, though I’d never say you’re wrong for disapproving the RTP style regardless of effort used on it. If it sounded that way, I definitely did not mean it that way.

posts.author: Iron_Brew
posts.body:
Let's get this thread back to its discussion:
I do think that the question posited by the OP and the thread at large is a subjective one. One man's meat is another man's poison, but I do think there are several metrics by which it's possible to judge any RPG as poor - and in RPG Maker games these are only easier to identify:
I don't wish to throw shade at individual RPG Maker games, because I think doing so only weakens us as a community, but I think it's easy enough to identify the facets of games which
could
undermine one's enjoyment of a game. So, why not look at these trends to see how we can avoid falling into these flaws and pitfalls ourselves?
Seems like a decent use of time that might get this thread back on track, eh?
Whether any of these make the game "Bad" is kind of too subjective to really touch on.
Poor Plot
Games whose stories make no sense, or are poor enough that they distract from the other gameplay elements. We see a lot of these in RPG Maker Land because the engine's core gameplay loop is kind of tried and tested, and
quite difficult to foul up
.
This point applies not only to the overall plot but to the way in which the plot is conveyed to the player. Pacing issues, plot holes, or "why didn't you read the 40 page worldbuilding document, it all makes sense if you memorise my fantasy world's rules" can all undermine an otherwise perfectly serviceable plot.
Under this heading I'd also count 'theming' - while I freely admit taht this is somewhat more subejctive, but there are a bunch of themes we see repeatedly dealt with here which have started to wear thin. This isn't to say that these themes are inherently bad, but there's only so many games with the theme "Parents are Bad", "Friendship can easily overcome Fascism", "Spooky Ghost School!" or "Friendship or "Persona 4 didn't have enough Sexual Assault" that one can reasonably play
Poor writing
By this I mean incidental moment-to-moment writing, distinct from 'plot' or 'worldbuilding'. The actual nuts and bolts of language which make language work (or not). I've lost count of the number of games with really great plots, fantastic worlds, and fun world and battle design only to be pulled out of it by poor writing.
Notably, this occurs just as much outside RPG Maker as it does inside -
Chained Echoes
is a game I literally couldn't finish in spite of being invested in the story, characters, world, and gameplay, but the moment-to-moment writing was so full of errors that it undermind the entire game.
Poor presentation
Going with "Poor Presentation" rather than "Bad Art" or "Bad Sound" here because I think it's a broader set of issues than 'omg he used an asset pack I dislike', or 'the RTP's art direction is bad'. Plenty of games have lacklustre art, or use the RTP, and look
fine to great,
so clearly the issues lie elsewhere.
The issue here tends to be one of
inconsistency
rather than 'bad art'. "Mapping", as we call it in RM isn't just 'the map is functional', or 'wow what a believable space' - maps should also be presented in an appealing way. They should look nice, have points of interest spaced in such a way that it's not over (or under) whelming to the player to enter a new area. It shouldn't contain assets with drastically differing artstyles, or be chock full of copy-pasted prefabs in a grid.
The same extends to the game's art as a whole - people often forget that your game's art doesn't end with "Map" and "Battle". Key art, UI art, battlebacks, CGs and cutscenes; all of these contribute to the look and feel of your project. If you're spending big in one place it can be jarring if the others look poor, and that can contribute to player friction.
My final point is in Sound - because everything I've said above about art is equally applicable to sound. Good direction trumps good individual assets, and cohesion/consistency is going to move the needle more than
one really good facet
while all the others are dross (or worse, generic).
TL;DR - good direction can often overcome suboptimal assets, and poor direction can take good assets and make them a weakness, rather than a strength.
Poor design
This is probably the hardest to define, and the most subejctive point in the list, but it's pretty easy to list some common issues seen in RPG Maker games with design:
Aesthetics over function - the idea that a game looking good/flashy is more important than the core function of the game. You see this all the time with people prioritising spectacle in Action Sequences that make battles take much longer than they need to, or people purchasing tilesets and then using them to make maps that do not work or are a pain to navigate.
Literally no attention paid to level design - "Mapping" does not just mean 'the dungeon has set dressing every 3 tiles'. Sight-lines for points of interest, brevity and condensing maps that see repeated travel, simply not making your maps "too big" for a sense of scale - all of these can really easily level up the moment-to-moment gameplay of any RPG, but for some reason we see so many games that
look great
but interacting with their world is a pain because they've not employed any level design fundamentals whatsoever.
"My Battle System is Great" - this is the one I see the most and it's a multi-faceted issue that is extremely far-reaching so bear with me here. There's a lot of ways that this manifests: From massive overcomplication in the numbers of states and skills you're expecting players to remember and manage, to overreliance on systemic solutions to content-based issues, it's the thing I wish RPG Maker users would focus on improving most. If your battles are as complex at Enemy 1 as they are at your Final Boss, you've designed your game in an inherently anti-player way. If you expect the player to know everything you do from the outset, you've designed your game in an anti-player way. If you have 400 elements and 500 custom states and the player has to remember all of them, that complexity may appeal to some people but for the mostpart it will be offputting. If all your battles are just
different numbers
with the same 5 Low's Battlers in varying hues, you're not actually designing engaging content. Which brings me onto my last point:
Systems Vs Content - A game with good systems is important - and well-designed systems are the backbone of a good game! The issue comes when that's the end of the things you design and you then fill the game with milquetoast content that isn't individually interesting. The default RPG Maker combat system is often described as "bad" or "boring" by its detractors, but with decent encounter design the default combat system can be incredibly entertianing. On the flipside, people often install complex and 'interesting' battle systems then fail to do anything iwth them thinking the systems will instill fun and carry their uninteresting combat through.
I'm sure there's facets and trends that I've missed, and that's what I'm curious to hear! What in your mind degrades a game? What sins do you think are unforgiveable that you'd love to see RM creators remedy?
We all have our blind spots, so discussing the things that we've noticed could help us identify problems in our own games innit!
Thanks for coming to my TED talk.

There's a difference between "passion to release the project" and "passion to make their project at least tolerable to everyone else".

The (poorly executed) "mystery box" opening.  I find that not even JJ Abrams executes Mystery Boxes well.  I don't expect rank amateurs to get something right that a famous TV Series guy messes up routinely.
Or, as it's probably more commonly known, the game starting "in media res".
I can't count the amount of RPG Maker games in particular that start the game "in battle" or shortly before a battle.  Or, start the game at the moment of some strange event.  This can work, but the people who make these decisions often forget the "set up" and the "focus" of these events.  As in, they don't contextualize the situation properly before and after the event.  It's just, "here's a fight for survival right at the beginning!".  Or, "here's a weird thing to try to hook you on premise!"
These can work, but for me, they often don't, and it just drives me crazy.
Too often these are paired with "the obtuse mechanics tutorial".  Here's how the stagger system works.  Here's how you do combat stuff.  Here's how the stealth works.  Whatever.  Now, do the thing exactly as told.
The other thing I think a "bad RPG Maker Game" does (which also annoys me) is that they don't focus on "making things dead" in combat.  The focus is on anything EXCEPT making the enemies dead.  A good combat system has a lot of depth for how you approach combat, but always results in you winning combat in under 10 seconds for regular enemies and under 5 minutes for bosses.  Flashy animations, managing mechanics, etcetera, should not extend these timers.  A fight isn't "more fun" because it's longer.  It isn't "more fun" because your boss has 2 phases and 10 mechanics to learn.
I am not playing a singleplayer RPG to engage with MMO mechanics that exist in an MMO to promote team play and interaction with other players.
Let's put the combat time thing in perspective:
If the numbers are still true from years ago (8 or more) when I calculated "length of dungeon" by encounters, you're looking at roughly 35 fights a dungeon on average.  Not including the boss fight.
If each encounter is 10 seconds, you're looking at 350 seconds of combat each dungeon.  Almost 6 minutes of combat.  Add to that, the 5 minutes of a boss fight, and you've got about 11 minutes of combat per dungeon.  How long does it take to traverse the dungeon itself on top of that?  Times vary wildly.  But, 10 minutes per dungeon seems okay, right?  What if it's another 5 minutes to traverse the whole dungeon?  Well, now it's 15 minutes per dungeon you're in.  If you have say... 20 dungeons...  5 hours of dungeon content right there.  Assuming all dungeons are created equal.  If your RPG is only 7 hours long...  Well, that's a good way to hit some burnout of your players on your combat system.
I play a lot of RPG's (RPG Maker and otherwise) where combat burnout is a very real thing that keeps me from continuing to play a game.
Combat being long in an MMO or multiplayer space makes sense.  In a singleplayer space, it makes no sense.
I tire of devs pulling MMO mechanics into singleplayer games.  There's a reason it exists in the MMO space.  It's because it works for that type of game.  You should leave it there.
